cards.back: A **survivorship curve** graphs the number or percent of a cohort still alive at each age. It starts with every newborn alive and slopes down as individuals die.

cards.front: What is a life history strategy?
cards.back: A **life history strategy** is a species' typical pattern of growth, reproduction, parental care and survival across its lifespan. It shows how the species divides its energy.
cards.hint: Think about how a species spends its energy over its life.

cards.front: Why do species end up with such different survivorship curves?
cards.back: Each species divides its energy differently. Few offspring with heavy care gives a Type I curve, while very many offspring with little care gives a Type III curve.
cards.hint: Compare the number of offspring with the amount of care each one gets.

cards.back: A **cohort** is a group of individuals of one species born during the same time period and followed through their lives.

cards.front: Why do most offspring of a Type I species survive to adulthood?
cards.back: **Parents guard the few young closely**, so most reach adulthood. Deaths rise sharply only near the end of the lifespan.
cards.hint: Think about the care each offspring receives.

cards.front: What shape does a Type II curve make on a logarithmic axis, and why?
cards.back: A **straight diagonal line**, because the chance of dying stays about the same at every age.

cards.front: What defines a Type III survivorship curve?
cards.back: Very high death rates **early in life**. The curve drops steeply on the left, then flattens, and survivors of the early stage often live much longer.
cards.hint: Compare where its steep section sits with a Type I curve.

cards.front: Which r-selected and K-selected groups match Type III and Type I curves?
cards.back: Type III species resemble **r-selected** species, which have many offspring and mature early. Type I species resemble **K-selected** species, which have few offspring and long lives. These are general trends, not strict rules.

cards.front: Why is a high Type I curve not caused by having many offspring?
cards.back: Type I species have **few offspring** with heavy care. The curve stays high because parents protect each young, not because the species produces large numbers.
cards.hint: Compare offspring number with the parental care column in the table.

cards.front: How do you read a survivorship curve to classify it?
cards.back: 1) Find the steepest section, where most deaths occur. 2) Name the curve type. 3) Link it to offspring number and parental care.
cards.hint: Look at the part of the graph that drops most, then think about biology.

cards.front: A cohort of 1,000 fish has 120 survivors at week 1. What percent of the cohort dies in week 1?
cards.back: $88\%$ of the cohort dies in week 1, which is 880 fish (1,000 − 120). Most deaths occur early, so the data fit a Type III curve.
cards.hint: Compare each loss with the number alive at the start of that interval.

cards.front: Counts fall from 1,000 to 500 to 250 over equal intervals. What percent is lost in each interval?
cards.back: $50\%$ is lost in each interval. A steady percent loss points to a Type II curve.
